REBUS in SilicoIntro

Loosening an over-fitted prior

A small recurrent network stands in for a brain and its training data for past experience. Overfit to a narrow past, its error on new data grows. Can a burst of hidden-unit noise, standing in for the rise in brain entropy reported under psychedelics, reduce that error, and why would noise help at all?

Scene 1

An over-fitted prior

A network overfit to a narrow past predicts new data less accurately.

Both the glowing network above and this landscape are illustrations, but every outcome and number the landscape shows comes from the real simulations.

Picture: A cross-section of the loss landscape comes out of the dark: a high shoulder with a narrow notch cut into it. A small glowing network hovers above it.

Psychedelics

In the canalization model, repeating the same narrow experience deepens a prior until new evidence no longer revises it. Here the network's training data plays the part of that experience.

Picture: The network gathers into a single point of light, which comes down to rest on the shoulder beside the notch. A panel under the sentence shows its data: filled dots for its old data, the training data, and open diamonds for new data, with a flat line for its prediction before any training. The old-data dots light up in turn, again and again: the same narrow experience, repeated.

The model

It is trained for 40,000 training steps on the same 32 sequences until it overfits. Its error on new sequences first falls, then rises as it fits the noise in its training data.

Picture: Training: the point slides down into the notch and swings back and forth there, each pass shorter, until it settles. In the panel the old-data dots go on lighting up in turn. The curve first finds the trend and comes close to both kinds of data; then each pass bends it closer to the old-data dots and further from the new data, until it runs exactly through every old dot. The notch is labelled narrow local minimum, and an arrow beside the picture reads: error on new data, lower is better.

Takeaway

Its training error is near zero, but its held-out error, on new sequences, is 18 times higher, nearly double its best early in training. In the analogy, that is a canalized prior.

Picture: In the panel the two kinds of miss are pointed out in turn. First the old data: each dot glows where the curve runs through it, with nothing between them. Then the new data: a bar from each diamond to the curve, and the bars are long. That miss on new data is the point's height.

Scene 2

The dose

The dose is a burst of noise added to every hidden unit during training.

Picture: The view draws back a little from the point in its notch. It begins to glow warm. The panel still shows its curve missing the new data.

Psychedelics

The entropic brain hypothesis holds that psychedelics raise the entropy of brain activity, and REBUS adds annealing, in which heat relaxes priors and cooling settles them into new ones.

Picture: The point stays a ball, but now it circles quickly through a wide cloud of light that lies on the ground around it, sparkling like the glowing network at the top of the page: the cloud is the spread of where its noisy steps take it. The cloud is too wide for the notch: it fills it, and its middle lifts out to rest on the shoulder above. A pale ring stays in the notch: the same network with no dose.

The model

The noise raises the entropy of the hidden activity while training continues. The gradient-descent path leaves the narrow minimum, and a deeper basin with lower held-out error comes into view.

Picture: The view pulls back, and a wide, deeper basin comes into sight for the first time. The cloud spills over the lip and pours down the long slope toward the basin. The ring stays in its notch. In the panel the curve smooths out: it lets go of the old-data dots, follows the trend, and its bars to the new data shrink, though not to nothing.

Takeaway

At its peak the dose cut the held-out error by over a third. As training on the old data continues, most of the gain is lost, yet the error ends 8% lower than with no dose.

Picture: The dose ends and the cloud condenses back into a point on the slope. A current of old data draws it back up toward the notch, most of the way, but it comes to rest lower than the ring. In the panel the curve picks up some of its bends again and the bars grow, though not all the way. The undosed network's curve is shown dashed behind it, still bent through every old-data dot; the dosed curve is plainly smoother and closer to the new data. Better: 8% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks.

Scene 3

What comes after

Does training on new data after the dose keep more of the gain?

Picture: Time winds back to the moment the dose ended: the point glides back down the slope to where the dose left it, still glowing. The panel leaves.

Psychedelics

REBUS stresses set, setting and integration. Like heated metal, a mind softened by the drug takes the shape of whatever works on it next.

Picture: The view moves in on the point where the dose left it, part-way down the slope. It is still soft and glowing, with a few sparks around it. Two faint currents wait beside it: one drawing back up toward the notch, one drawing down toward the basin.

The model

After the same dose, training continues on the old training set, on old plus 32 new sequences, or on unlimited new data, standing in for the life that follows.

Picture: The picture opens into three lanes, one for each thing the network learns from: old data, old plus new data, or unlimited new data. Each lane starts where its own run was when the dose ended. With old data the ring is still in the notch, and the current draws the point most of the way back to it. With old plus new data both marks were already out of the notch, and both are drawn part of the way back up the slope, the dosed point staying lower. With unlimited new data both marks were already near the basin floor, and they stay there.

Takeaway

Here training on 32 extra sequences keeps more of the gain. With unlimited new data the dose leaves no lasting benefit, even a slight cost, and the undosed network ends with slightly lower held-out error.

Picture: Each lane shows its result as the gap between the dosed point and the ring. Old data: Better: 8% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks. Old plus new data: Better: 11% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks. Unlimited new data: Worse: 0.2% higher held-out error than no dose; 8 of 20 networks did better.

Scene 4

Plasticity and age

Does a higher learning rate after the dose keep more of the gain?

Picture: One picture again: the lane with old plus new data grows to fill the stage, and time winds back to the moment its dose ended. The point is part-way down the slope; the ring, which also left the notch, a little above it.

Psychedelics

Plasticity generally declines with age (5-HT2A receptor density is highest early in life), and psychedelics are thought to reopen it for a while. Here the learning rate stands for plasticity.

Picture: The view moves in on the point. It turns molten: large, soft, amber and wobbling, as plastic as a young network. A cue beside it reads: learning rate, falling with aging. Then, as it ages, it cools and shrinks toward a small, pale, hard-edged bead: by the end of the dose its plasticity is about a fifth of what it was.

The model

Without aging the learning rate stays at 0.03 after the dose. With aging it keeps falling, from 0.01 toward 0.002, so each training step changes the weights less and less.

Picture: Two lanes open, each starting where its own run was when the dose ended: the same dose in a network that does not age, above, and in one that does, below. Both points are pulled back up the slope. Without aging the point stays molten and slides nearly all the way back to the notch. With aging it goes on hardening, moves less than half as far, and stops much lower down.

Takeaway

No. At a high learning rate, later training pulls both networks back toward the narrow minimum, leaving the dosed one only 5% lower in held-out error. With aging that pull fades and it ends 11% lower, like a mind whose declining plasticity keeps the change.

Picture: Each lane shows its result as the gap between the dosed point and the ring. No aging: Better: 5% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks. Aging: Better: 11% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks.

Scene 5

Why it works

Does the noise help by exploring, or by smoothing?

Picture: One picture again, back at the start of the dose: the cloud hovers over its notch. A dashed line now shows the ground as the cloud feels it, the average of the ground beneath it. In that line the notch is gone.

Psychedelics

REBUS reads the effect statistically, as flattening sharp minima "to reduce model complexity and preclude overfitting". Averaged over the noise, a narrow minimum is smoothed away while a wide basin survives.

Picture: The view pulls back to the whole landscape. The dashed line runs on down the slope and into the wide basin: averaging has flattened the narrow notch away, but the basin is still there.

The model

A noise-free smoothing penalty added to the training loss leaves the narrow minimum just as the noise does, while doubling the learning rate, which the canalization model's TEMP groups with entropy, only takes bigger steps inside it.

Picture: Three lanes open, one per treatment, each at the start of its dose. Noise dose: the cloud and its dashed line. Noise-free stand-in: no cloud, only a point, but it is given the same dashed line to follow. Learning-rate boost: a molten point, and the notch as sharp as ever. Then the doses play. The cloud pours out of the notch and down the slope. The noise-free point, following its line, leaves the same way and goes just as far. The boosted point takes long strides from wall to wall inside the notch and never leaves it.

Takeaway

The smoothing penalty does as well as the noise with no rise in entropy, and the learning-rate boost alone does not help, ending slightly worse here. The noise helps by smoothing, not by exploring.

Picture: The doses end. The old-data current draws the two escaped points most of the way back, and each rests lower than its ring by about the same gap. The boosted point never left. Noise dose: Better: 8% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks. Noise-free stand-in: Better: 9% lower held-out error than no dose, in 20 of 20 networks. Learning-rate boost: Worse: 0.2% higher held-out error than no dose; 1 of 20 networks did better.

Novel predictions

If brains work like this model, it makes six predictions that, as far as we found, the published theory does not; each is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.

  1. 1. Rich new experience makes the dose redundant.

    PredictionBeyond a little, the more genuinely new experience follows a session, the smaller the lasting difference between drug and placebo, until it disappears.

    TestA drug × post-session experience trial with three arms: the usual routine, a small programme of new activities, and an intensive one.

    Open in the explorer

  2. 2. Plasticity that keeps falling makes the change last.

    PredictionA dose's benefit fades more slowly where plasticity keeps declining after it, and a later dose, given when plasticity is already low, leaves less lasting benefit.

    TestDose young-adult and aged rodents, and the same strain early or late in adulthood, then compare the drug–saline difference at one week and two months.

    Open in the explorer

  3. 3. More plasticity alone does not help.

    PredictionA drug that raises plasticity without raising entropy gives little or no lasting benefit, and after a small set of new experiences can leave people slightly worse off.

    TestCompare a non-hallucinogenic plasticity promoter (tabernanthalog, in rodents), a classic psychedelic and placebo, each followed by the same limited new training.

    Open in the explorer

  4. 4. Entropy dips below baseline as the drug wears off.

    PredictionResting brain entropy falls briefly below placebo as acute effects end: deeper after a short, intense dose or an abrupt stop than after a long, tapered one.

    TestRecord resting EEG LZc densely through the hours after a DMT bolus, a long infusion and a tapered infusion, each against placebo.

    Open in the explorer

  5. 5. A lasting entropy rise does not mark lasting benefit.

    PredictionA lasting rise in resting entropy after a dose appears mainly in less plastic, for example older, people whose life afterwards is rich in new experience, and it does not track benefit.

    TestIn a drug vs placebo trial, record resting LZc at one and three months, stratified by age, with an intensive new-activities programme for half of each group.

    Open in the explorer

  6. 6. How high entropy rises during a session does not predict who benefits.

    PredictionThe size of the acute entropy rise does not predict lasting benefit once the dose itself is fixed. In the model the evidence is a weak null: ρ = −0.17 (interval −0.35 to +0.02) across 160 toy networks, which rules out a clear positive link but not a modest negative one.

    TestCorrelate the acute LZc rise with outcome across people given the same dose and setting; the model predicts no reliable link.

    Open in the explorer

Appendix

A simulation: a toy network and synthetic data. Nothing on this page is evidence about brains or therapy.
